comparator.name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE)
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from VU Amsterdam's current official sources for the Fall-2026 cohort: the Bachelor Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) curriculum page, its future/career page, and the PPE 2026-2027 Teaching and Examination Regulations (TER/OER), the formally adopted regulation governing the programme (Article 7.1: RIO number 54999, offered jointly by the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities and the School of Business and Economics, hosted by J.S. Mill College). Article 10.2 names three specialisations -- Philosophy, Politics, Economics -- and requires every student to follow exactly two of them (Article 11.4); the normalized target is the generic 'B Philosophy, Politics and Economics' bachelor and does not name a specific pair. All three pairings (Philosophy & Economics; Philosophy & Political Science; Political Science & Economics) require the same 90 EC of Year-1 common units, the same 12 EC of shared Year-2 PPE-in-Practice units, and the same Year-3 structure, and none is named as more representative of the programme's broad academic identity than another by the curriculum page, the future page or the OER's own Article 10.1 objective statement, which describes the three disciplines symmetrically. No pairing is less specialised than another either: each combines exactly two of the three disciplines to the same 6 EC x 2 compulsory + 24 EC elective depth. The OER's own Appendix 1 (Programme overview) prints three annual-plan tables in one fixed order -- 'TRACKS PHILOSOPHY & ECONOMICS' first, 'TRACKS PHILOSOPHY & POLITICAL SCIENCE' second, 'TRACKS POLITICAL SCIENCE & ECONOMICS' third -- so the official-order tie-break selects the first-listed pairing, Philosophy & Economics, fixed before any UCR course was considered. Year 1 (Article 11.3, common to all students, 60 EC): Ethics (W_JSM_101), Methods of PPE I (W_JSM_102), Political Science: State, Power, Conflict (W_JSM_104), PPE in Practice I: Wellbeing, Politics and Markets (W_JSM_105), History of Philosophy (W_JSM_106), Methods of PPE II (W_JSM_107), Foundations of Microeconomics (W_JSM_108), Comparative Politics (W_JSM_109), PPE in Practice II: From Theory to Practice (W_JSM_110), Foundations of Macroeconomics (W_JSM_111). Year 2 (60 EC): PPE in Practice III: Governance for Society (W_JSM_207) and PPE in Practice IV: Connected World (W_JSM_208) are common to all students; Article 11.4 requires the two compulsory units of each chosen specialisation, so the Philosophy specialisation's Philosophy of Science (W_JSM_201) and Political Philosophy (W_JSM_204) and the Economics specialisation's Micro-economics and Methods (W_JSM_203) and Macro-economics and Policy (W_JSM_206) are compulsory; Article 11.4 also requires four electives from the chosen specialisations with at least one per specialisation. Target-specific programme-interest evidence corroborates three of the four Philosophy electives individually (Ethics II: Autonomy, Freedom and Responsibility, row 5112; Epistemology, row 5114; Political Philosophy II: Global Justice, row 5113) but no Economics elective individually, so those three Philosophy electives are instantiated on that specific evidence and the OER's own listed order (Article 12, elective annex) is used as the neutral tie-break for the fourth, Economics-side elective, selecting the first-listed Economics elective, International Trade and Development Economics (W_JSM_219). Year 3 (60 EC): Article 11.5 lists Tutorial PPE (W_JSM_304, 6 EC) and Thesis PPE (W_JSM_SCR, 12 EC); Article 9.1 requires 108 EC of Year-1/2 courses by period 3 before the thesis may be taken. Article 11.4 offers Methods of PPE III or Methods of PPE IV: Qualitative Research Methods (both W_JSM_305/306, 6 EC); target-specific evidence (row 5124, 'qualitative social research', explicit: 'the third year includes qualitative research methods') supports instantiating the qualitative option, W_JSM_306. Article 12.2a gives the first semester of Year 3 as genuine open profiling space (30 EC): a bilateral or VU-wide study abroad exchange, an approved internship (minimum 840 hours, W_JSM_STA), or an approved 30-EC package of electives/minor (at least 18 EC at level 300) -- no single content is fixed by the OER, so it is preserved as open space rather than instantiated. PPE in Practice V: Advanced Topics (W_JSM_302, 6 EC) is common to all students. 60 (Year 1) + 60 (Year 2) + 60 (Year 3) = 180 EC. No further official source needed to be consulted: the curriculum page, future page and OER together establish a complete, internally consistent, entirely accounted-for 180-EC pathway with explicit EC weights and compulsory/elective status for every component, and an explicit, UCR-independent route- and elective-selection judgment fixed before any UCR course was considered.

routeSelection.basis: OER Article 10.2 names three specialisations (Philosophy, Politics, Economics) and Article 11.4 requires every student to follow exactly two of them; the normalized target is the generic bachelor and names no specific pair. All three pairings share an identical 90 EC of Year-1/shared-Year-2 common units and an identical Year-3 structure, and combine exactly two disciplines to the same depth (2 compulsory + electives per chosen specialisation), so no pairing is more representative of the programme's broad academic identity, and none is less specialised, than another under the curriculum page, future page or OER Article 10.1's own symmetric description of the three disciplines. The OER's Appendix 1 (Programme overview) prints exactly three annual-plan tables in a fixed order -- 'TRACKS PHILOSOPHY & ECONOMICS', then 'TRACKS PHILOSOPHY & POLITICAL SCIENCE', then 'TRACKS POLITICAL SCIENCE & ECONOMICS' -- so the official-order tie-break selects the first-listed pairing, Philosophy & Economics, fixed before any UCR course was considered and independent of UCR fit.

core: PPE's integrated multidisciplinary identity: examining complex societal problems through combined philosophy, political-science and economics perspectives
Evaluating and constructing solutions to urgent societal challenges using multiple disciplinary lenses together
Ethical reasoning applied to public policy and social choices, and the history of philosophical ideas grounding it
Political science foundations shared by every PPE student regardless of chosen tracks: the state, power, political conflict, and comparative political systems
Microeconomic and macroeconomic foundations shared by every PPE student, and how markets, wellbeing and public choice interact
Philosophy as a formal Year-2 specialisation: political philosophy, the ethics of autonomy and responsibility, epistemology, philosophy of science and the history of philosophy
Economics as a formal Year-2 specialisation: micro/macro-economic methods and policy, behavioural, public and international-trade economics
Formal mathematical, statistical and logical methods -- including decision theory and rigorous argument -- trained across the Methods of PPE sequence
Independent interdisciplinary research culminating in a PPE bachelor thesis
Combining two of PPE's three disciplines in structural depth, as VU's own Year-2 specialisation requires of every student

questions: How should climate change, migration, AI and international development be governed, and what do economics, political institutions and ethics each contribute to that policy analysis?

What professional and career directions -- policymaking, political leadership, think-tank and policy consulting, journalism and academic research -- does a combined philosophy-politics-economics training prepare graduates for?

alternatives.label: Philosophy & Economics: Ethics, Markets and Public Choice
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by two clusters mirroring the exact Philosophy & Economics track pairing selected for the comparator: economics (6 of 24 courses: Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior, Public Economics, Econometrics, Behavioral Economics) and philosophy (5 of 24: Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Emotion, Free Will, Time & the Self), together with the shared Year-1 political-science foundation every PPE student takes regardless of chosen tracks (2 of 24: Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics), a mathematics/statistics/logic methods cluster (4 of 24: Research Methods & Statistics, Mathematical Methods, Probability & Statistics, Logic & Discrete Mathematics), a sociology/law/communication cluster implementing PPE's applied interdisciplinary policy-analysis strand (5 of 24: Introduction to Sociology, Qualitative Research Methodology, Modern Sociology, Persuasive Communication, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy) and Personal & Professional Development. The label names Philosophy and Economics first because those are the two disciplines the curriculum studies in genuine depth, mirroring VU's own track pairing, and names ethics, markets and public choice because those are the substantive threads -- ethical reasoning, economic analysis of markets, and the public/political choices both disciplines jointly evaluate -- that the completed curriculum's philosophy and economics clusters actually pursue together.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to VU's PPE bachelor, reconstructing the exact Philosophy & Economics track pairing selected for the comparator: UCR's Philosophy and Economics course clusters, the shared first-year political-science and quantitative-methods/logic foundation every PPE student takes regardless of track, and a sociology, law and persuasive-communication strand reproducing PPE's applied interdisciplinary policy-analysis strand (PPE in Practice; ethical decision-making in public policy). It honestly preserves that UCR offers no integrated Methods-of-PPE sequence combining all three disciplines' methods in one course, no second/advanced political-philosophy or philosophy-of-science course, and no bachelor thesis comparable to VU's own.
progression: No UCR course in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite except the courses that require BENGATE102 (BENECON211, BENECON212, BENECON311, BENECON312, BENECON314) and DISGATE102 (DISMATH314, DISMATH214); BENGATE102 and DISGATE102 are both scheduled in semester 2, before every course that depends on them. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 2, within Year 1. Introductory Year-1 courses (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Introduction to Economics) are concentrated in semester 1, and level-3 advanced work (Public Economics, Philosophy of Emotion, Free Will Time & the Self, Econometrics, Behavioral Economics) is concentrated in semesters 4-6, so foundational training precedes advanced work. Where an advisory continuation exists in the course evidence, it is honoured: Introduction to Western Philosophy (semester 1) precedes the more advanced Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Emotion and Free Will, Time & the Self (semesters 4/4/5); Ethics (semester 2) precedes the thematically continuous Free Will, Time & the Self (semester 5); Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes the more advanced Probability & Statistics and Qualitative Research Methodology (semesters 3/6); and Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes the more advanced Advanced Calculus (semester 6). Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.

alternatives.label: Political Economy & Global Governance
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by political science (5 of 24: Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict) and economics (6 of 24, identical to the closest match's own economics cluster: Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior, Public Economics, Econometrics, Behavioral Economics), together with a law/governance cluster (3 of 24: Law, Society & Justice, Introduction to Public International Law, Comparative Constitutional Law) and a history cluster (3 of 24: Modern History, History of Empires, Western Way of War) studying the institutional and historical foundations of power and governance, a methods/quantitative cluster (4 of 24: Research Methods & Statistics, Mathematical Methods, Probability & Statistics, Linear Algebra), one applied course on social movements and environmental justice, and Personal & Professional Development. The label names political economy first because political science and economics -- the two disciplines VU's own third official track pairing combines -- are what the curriculum studies in genuine depth, and names global governance because the law, history and social-movements courses together study how power, institutions and policy operate across borders, the substantive thread the completed curriculum actually pursues beyond the two named disciplines.
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different second UCR route evidenced by VU's own Political Science & Economics track pairing (the OER's third official annual-plan combination) and by target-specific evidence that PPE students structurally combine two disciplines in depth and pursue a recurring applied interdisciplinary policy-analysis line: UCR's Political Science course cluster (international relations, EU politics, peace and conflict), the same Economics cluster used in the closest match, and a law/history complementary strand implementing PPE's governance, global-connectivity and international-security territory. It honestly preserves that UCR does not offer PPE's own named Political Institutions, Global Governance and International Relations, Comparative Politics II or Global Political Economy units.
progression: No UCR course in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite except the courses that require BENGATE102 (BENECON211, BENECON212, BENECON311, BENECON312, BENECON314), DISGATE102 (DISMATH314, DISMATH211) and GOSGATE102 (GOSLAWJ212, GOSLAWJ213); BENGATE102 and DISGATE102 are scheduled in semester 2, and GOSGATE102 in semester 3, each before every course that depends on it. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 1, within Year 1. Introductory Year-1 courses are concentrated in semester 1, and level-3 advanced work (European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict, Public Economics, Econometrics, Behavioral Economics) is concentrated in semesters 4-6. Where an advisory continuation exists, it is honoured: Foundations of Comparative Politics (semester 1) precedes the more advanced Theory of International Relations (semester 2), European Union Politics (semester 5) and Peace & Conflict (semester 6); Law, Society & Justice (semester 3) precedes the more advanced Introduction to Public International Law and Comparative Constitutional Law (semester 4), both of which formally require it; and Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes the more advanced Linear Algebra (semester 3). Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.
alternatives.distinctness: VU's own OER structurally requires every PPE student to combine exactly two of Philosophy, Politics and Economics (Article 11.4); the closest match instantiates one such pairing (Philosophy & Economics, matching the comparator's own official-order tie-break). This alternative instantiates a second, equally official VU pairing -- Political Science & Economics, the OER's third annual-plan combination -- replacing the closest match's Philosophy cluster (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Emotion, Free Will Time & the Self) and its sociology/communication/law-adjacent applied strand (Introduction to Sociology, Modern Sociology, Persuasive Communication, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy, Qualitative Research Methodology) with a Political Science specialisation (Theory of International Relations, European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict) and a law/history strand implementing governance, global connectivity and international security (Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Public International Law, Comparative Constitutional Law, Modern History, History of Empires, Western Way of War, Social Movements & Environmental Justice, Linear Algebra). This is a material curricular consequence, not cosmetic reshuffling: it changes the alternative's academic priorities from ethics/epistemology-grounded policy analysis to institutional/international-governance-grounded policy analysis, mirroring the material difference between VU's own Philosophy and Political-Science specialisation learning outcomes (OER Article 10.3). The two alternatives share 13 of 24 courses -- the full Economics cluster and shared methods/logic courses that both of VU's own official track pairings require identically, plus the two shared Year-1 political-science foundation courses -- and differ in 11 of 24 courses each way (82.5 EC), well above the pairwise 30-EC/4-course minimum.

selection.assessment: The closest match directly owns eleven generator-eligible rows: PPE's integrated multidisciplinary identity and its societal-problem-solving and ethical-policy purpose (5102, 5103, 5104); the shared Year-1 political-science and economics foundation every PPE student takes (5105, 5106); Philosophy and Economics named individually as tracks, both instantiated in depth by the closest match (5107, 5109); the structural requirement to combine two disciplines in depth, which the closest match itself instantiates via Philosophy & Economics (5110); and formal mathematical/statistical/logical methods and independent interdisciplinary research (5122, 5123, 5125). The remaining two generator-eligible rows -- Politics named individually as a track (5108) and applied interdisciplinary policy analysis (5111) -- were independently assessed as one coherent candidate direction, 'Political Economy & Global Governance', because together they describe VU's own second official track pairing (Political Science & Economics) rather than the Philosophy & Economics pairing the closest match instantiates. This candidate passes all four gates: it is evidence-backed by two generator-eligible rows plus target-specific curricular-topic support (governance for society, global connectivity, comparative politics, micro/macro-economics); it has a clear organising logic (institutional/international-governance-grounded policy analysis via Politics & Economics rather than ethics/epistemology-grounded policy analysis via Philosophy & Economics); it is substantively distinct, replacing 11 of 24 courses and changing the alternative's academic priorities in a way that mirrors VU's own differing Philosophy and Political-Science learning outcomes; and it is mechanically feasible against the enriched course database, with 11 distinct courses (82.5 EC) each way against the closest match, well above the pairwise 30-EC/4-course floor. Production therefore includes it as the second alternative. A third candidate, 'Philosophy & Political Theory' -- VU's remaining official pairing, Philosophy & Political Science -- was then assessed and rejected as not-substantively-distinct: it would necessarily reuse most of the closest match's Philosophy cluster (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Emotion, Free Will Time & the Self -- UCR's entire relevant Philosophy catalogue, already exhausted by the closest match) and most of the second alternative's Political Science cluster (Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict -- UCR's entire relevant Political Science catalogue, already exhausted by the second alternative), leaving no genuinely new disciplinary content to build a third 24-course curriculum from without importing unrelated departments (data science, environment, media) merely to force numerical distinctness against both already-included alternatives simultaneously, or without arbitrary course substitutions that are not genuine consequences of an evidenced concept. Because its own evidence is already substantively covered between the two included alternatives and no genuinely different 24-course curriculum follows from it given UCR's actual course offerings, it is rejected as not-substantively-distinct rather than manufactured through arbitrary substitution, and production stops at two included alternatives.

blocks: Both are the general introductory research-methodology and statistics unit: Methods of PPE I is VU's own foundational methods course; Research Methods & Statistics covers the logics and design of research, operationalisation, sampling and descriptive/inferential statistics.

Both continue the shared methods sequence with a mathematical/quantitative emphasis: Methods of PPE II is VU's own second methods unit; Mathematical Methods trains the calculus, algebra and problem-solving techniques PPE's own mathematics-heavy economics relies on.

Both introduce the central questions, methods and history of Western philosophical thought: History of Philosophy is VU's own compulsory Year-1 unit; Introduction to Western Philosophy grounds the same territory before the Philosophy specialisation's advanced work.
Both are the compulsory Year-1 ethics unit: Ethics is VU's own unit; UCR's Ethics course examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism, the same central theories.

Philosophy of Science is VU's compulsory Philosophy-specialisation unit on the logical structure and methodology of scientific inquiry. Logic & Discrete Mathematics addresses an important and identifiable part of that subject -- the formal logic and rigorous argument underlying scientific reasoning -- even though it does not reproduce the full history-and-philosophy-of-science scope VU's own unit covers.

Both examine autonomy, free will and personal responsibility: Ethics II: Autonomy, Freedom and Responsibility is VU's own elective; Free Will, Time & the Self investigates free will, agency and the openness of the future.

Philosophy of Mind's investigation of consciousness, personal identity and the mind-body problem directly overlaps the Epistemology elective's central theory-of-knowledge questions about what the mind can know and how.

Both study global justice: Political Philosophy II: Global Justice is VU's own elective; Human Rights: Law & Philosophy studies human rights through legal, historical and philosophical perspectives, the same global-justice territory from a rights-based angle.

Political Philosophy is VU's compulsory Year-2 Philosophy-specialisation unit, distinct from and more advanced than the Year-1 Introduction to Political Philosophy already matched to the shared Political Science: State, Power, Conflict foundation below. UCR's catalogue contains no second, more advanced political-philosophy course, so no counterpart is claimed.

Both examine the state, political authority, power and conflict: Political Science: State, Power, Conflict is VU's own compulsory Year-1 unit taken by every PPE student; Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential thinkers' views on political authority and the state.

Both are the compulsory Year-1 comparative-politics unit taken by every PPE student: Comparative Politics is VU's own unit; Foundations of Comparative Politics compares political systems and institutional change across countries.

Foundations of Microeconomics is VU's own compulsory Year-1 unit. Introduction to Economics is the strongest available counterpart, covering introductory microeconomics (supply and demand, consumer and firm theory) and macroeconomics together; because it is already matched here, it cannot also be matched to Foundations of Macroeconomics below.

Foundations of Macroeconomics is VU's second compulsory Year-1 economics unit. Introduction to Economics, UCR's only introductory economics course, is already matched to Foundations of Microeconomics above and cannot be matched twice; no further UCR counterpart addresses introductory macroeconomics specifically.

Both are the compulsory Year-2 Economics-specialisation microeconomics unit: Micro-economics and Methods is VU's own unit; Microeconomics & Behavior deepens consumer behaviour, market structure and behavioural microeconomics beyond the Year-1 introduction.

Both examine macroeconomic policy: Macro-economics and Policy is VU's own compulsory Year-2 unit; International Macroeconomics examines national income, growth, business cycles and fiscal/monetary policy.

International Trade and Development Economics is the fourth Year-2 elective instantiated for the comparator. UCR's catalogue contains no dedicated international-trade or development-economics course; International Macroeconomics above already covers the general macroeconomic-policy territory and is matched to Macro-economics and Policy, so no further counterpart is claimed.
Applied interdisciplinary policy analysis (PPE in Practice)

PPE in Practice I: Wellbeing, Politics and Markets is a broad integrated Year-1 unit combining all three PPE disciplines on a concrete societal theme. UCR's catalogue contains no comparably integrated cross-disciplinary applications course; treating a single-discipline UCR course as a direct substitute would overstate what it actually reproduces, so no counterpart is claimed.
PPE in Practice II: From Theory to Practice is a second broad integrated Year-1 applications unit. For the same reason as PPE in Practice I above, no UCR counterpart is claimed.

PPE in Practice III: Governance for Society is a broad integrated unit on how society is governed. Law, Society & Justice addresses an important and identifiable part of that subject -- the legal, social and normative perspectives on governance -- even though it does not reproduce the unit's full interdisciplinary PPE framing.

PPE in Practice IV: Connected World is VU's unit on global interdependence and connectivity. Introduction to Public International Law directly addresses how legal order governs a connected world, an important and identifiable part of that theme.

PPE in Practice V: Advanced Topics is a broad, integrated Year-3 unit applying PPE's disciplines to advanced real-world problems. Social Movements & Environmental Justice is the strongest available counterpart, an advanced applied course on exactly the kind of urgent governance problem (climate and environmental policy) PPE's own career material identifies, even though it does not reproduce the unit's full interdisciplinary PPE scope.

Both are the Year-3 qualitative-methods unit: Methods of PPE IV: Qualitative Research Methods is VU's own unit (selected over the quantitative Methods of PPE III on target-specific evidence); Qualitative Research Methodology trains qualitative research design and interview-based methods.
Tutorial PPE is a small-group, supervised academic seminar preparing students for the thesis. UCR's catalogue contains no comparable supervised tutorial/seminar course, so no counterpart is claimed.

The 30-EC first-semester Year-3 profiling space (OER Article 12.2a: study abroad, an approved internship, or an approved 30-EC elective/minor package) is genuine open space with no fixed content specified by VU. It is preserved as open space and not matched to any UCR course.

Thesis PPE is the 12-EC independent bachelor thesis (OER Article 9.1 requires 108 EC of Year-1/2 units completed by period 3 of Year 3 before enrolment). No scheduled UCR course is a thesis; UCR's standardised Optional independent research element is shown in this row instead, consistent with researchComponentId.

notes.text: Philosophy, Politics and Economics combines a dedicated multidisciplinary curriculum -- compulsory Year-1 units in all three disciplines, a formal Year-2 specialisation in two of them, an integrated Methods-of-PPE sequence, a recurring PPE-in-Practice applications line and a bachelor thesis -- with a single-institution, single-college teaching structure. At UCR, students can approach the same combination of ethics, political institutions and economic analysis through separate Philosophy, Political Science, Economics, Sociology, Law and History courses. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives on PPE's central questions rather than reproducing a single integrated PPE curriculum or its own Methods-of-PPE sequence and thesis.
